questions_and_answers.question_text: When do you use the (Verb) de shi construction?
What kind of sentence does the (Verb) de shi pattern make?
In which three places may a guānyú phrase occur?
Where does guānyú NOT occur, unlike other prepositional verbs?
Where does the gěi phrase go when jiè means "to lend"?
Write the Chinese for "What is it that you study at the University of California?"

answers.answer_text: Nǐ zài Jiāzhōu Dàxué niànde shi shénme?

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Concerning that matter, I don't know anything."

answers.answer_text: Guānyú nèijiàn shì, wǒ shénme dōu bù zhīdào.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is the verb xiě not new information in sentence 2A?

answers.answer_text: Because any novel must "be written about" something — the new information is the object, dàlùde qíngkuàng.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Lend me a pen" in both forms.

answers.answer_text: Jiè wo yìzhī bǐ, or Jiè gěi wo yìzhī bǐ.
Rather formal — in everyday speech, "about" is more often expressed in other ways.

articles.text:
2. A: Zhèiběn xiǎoshuō xiěde shi     This novel is about the situation
      dàlùde qíngkuàng.               on the mainland.
   B: Guānyú dàlùde? Jiè gěi wo      About the mainland? How about
      kànkan xíng bu xíng?            lending it to me to read?

Notes on No. 2

xiě: This verb which you learned as "to write" is also one of several ways that "about" is expressed in Chinese. When used with this meaning, xiě usually appears in the (Verb)de shi construction discussed below.

xiěde shi: This structure, (Verb) de shi, is a MAJOR STRUCTURE of Chinese, so pay extra attention! Use (Verb) de shi when the verb is not new information and you want to focus instead on the identity of the thing talked about. The pattern itself makes an EQUATIONAL sentence, that is, an A EQUALS B sentence:

    A                    =        B
    (VERB) de           shi       B

In sentence 2A, the verb xiě is not new information because any novel must "be written about" something. The object dàlùde qíngkuàng is new information which is focused on.

A: Nǐ zài Jiāzhōu Dàxué niànde   What is it that you study at the
   shi shénme?                   University of California?
B: Wǒ niànde shi jīngjìxué.      It's economics.

Zhèige diànyǐng jiǎngde shi      This film is about a Chinese going
yíge Zhōngguo rén qù Měiguo      to America to visit.
wánde shì.
Gāngcái nǐ jiàode shi shénme?    What did you order just now? Rice
Shi fàn háishi miàn?             or noodles?
Tā hěn xǐhuan kàn shū, kěshi tā  He likes to read, but all he reads
kànde dōu shi yìxiē méi yìside   are stupid novels.
xiǎoshuō.

dàlù: "continent, mainland." Zhōngguó dàlù is "mainland China," which may also be called dàlù for short.

qíngkuàng: "situation, circumstances, state of affairs, condition." Used much more frequently in Chinese than any single one of these translations is used in English. Sometimes the Chinese language uses qíngkuàng when in English we would just say "things" or "the way things are."

Nǐde qíngkuàng gēn tāde          You and he are in about the same
chàbuduō.                        situation.
Nà shi sìshinián qiánde shì,     That was forty years ago. Now
xiànzài qíngkuàng bù tóng le.    things are different.
Wǒ bú tài shóuxi Měidàsīde       I'm not too familiar with (the way
qíngkuàng.                       things are at) the Department of
                                 American and Oceanic Affairs.

guānyú: "with regard to, concerning." Guānyú is rather formal. In everyday speech, the idea of "about" is more often expressed in other ways, but guānyú is often used in formal contexts.

Guānyú is a PREPOSITIONAL VERB, but it is not the best behaved of prepositional verbs. Guānyú does NOT occur where you would normally expect to find a prepositional verb phrase (before the verb). Nor does guānyú occur in a sentence the way "about" does in English. A guānyú phrase can only occur in the following places:

(1) At the BEGINNING of the sentence, to introduce the topic.

Guānyú nèijiàn shì, wǒ shénme    Concerning that matter, I don't know
dōu bù zhīdào.                   anything.
Guānyú zhèige, nǐmen hái yǒu     Do you have any other questions about
méiyou shénme wèntí?             this?

(2) In a phrase with -de which MODIFIES A NOUN.

Xièxie ni gàosu wo zhème duō     Thank you for telling me so much about
guānyú dàlùde qíngkuàng.         the situation on the mainland.
Wǒmen zhèli méiyou duōshao       We don't have very many books about
guānyú Zhōngguóde shū.           China here.

(3) Occasionally used ALONE as an abbreviated sentence.

Shénme diànyǐng?                 About what?
Guānyú Fǎguó...                  About France...
Guānyú Fǎguóde jīngjì.           About the French economy.

Although the parts in parentheses are optional in English, the Chinese sentences would be considered WRONG without the -de phrases:

Nǐ tīngshuō guānyú Tiětuōde      Have you heard (the news) about Tito?
xiāoxi ma?
Bú yào wèn wo guānyú shùxuéde    Don't ask me (any questions) about
wèntí.                           math.

jiè gěi wo kànkan: "lend (it) to me to read." In exchange 1, jiè was translated "borrow." Now you see it used for "to lend." To say "lend something to someone," the gěi phrase always FOLLOWS the verb jiè. If the indirect object is a pronoun, gěi may be omitted:

Jiè wo yìzhī bǐ.                 Lend me a pen.
Jiè gěi wo yìzhī bǐ.
